summary.text: At \(n=140\), direct floor evaluations give \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\), with the square-root bounds justified by squaring positive quantities. Thus the proposed right-hand side is \(528+484-471=541\), not \(a(161)=542\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor
\qquad(n\ge 1).
\]
We disprove the proposed recurrence by evaluating it at the single admissible index \(n=140\). At that index the conjecture asserts
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
We will compute all four terms exactly.

First, we record how the square-root floor calculations will be justified. For positive integers \(m\) and nonnegative integers \(k\), both \(m\sqrt{5/4}\) and \(k\) are nonnegative. Consequently,
\[
k\le m\sqrt{\frac54}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
k^2\le m^2\frac54
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
4k^2\le 5m^2.
\]
Likewise, because both sides are nonnegative,
\[
m\sqrt{\frac54}<k+1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
m^2\frac54<(k+1)^2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
5m^2<4(k+1)^2.
\]
Thus, to prove
\(\lfloor m\sqrt{5/4}\rfloor=k\), it suffices to establish the two integer inequalities
\[
4k^2\le 5m^2<4(k+1)^2.
\]

We now apply this criterion to the four required indices.

For \(m=140\) and \(k=156\), direct integer arithmetic gives
\[
4\cdot156^2=97344,
\qquad
5\cdot140^2=98000,
\qquad
4\cdot157^2=98596.
\]
Hence
\[
97344\le 98000<98596,
\]
so
\[
156\le 140\sqrt{\frac54}<157
\]
and therefore
\[
\left\lfloor140\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=156.
\]
Also \(140=4\cdot35\), so \(\lfloor140/4\rfloor=35\). It follows that
\[
a(140)=2\cdot140+156+35=280+156+35=471.
\]

For \(m=144\) and \(k=160\), we have
\[
4\cdot160^2=102400,
\qquad
5\cdot144^2=103680,
\qquad
4\cdot161^2=103684.
\]
Thus
\[
102400\le103680<103684,
\]
which implies
\[
160\le144\sqrt{\frac54}<161.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\left\lfloor144\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=160.
\]
Since \(144=4\cdot36\), we also have \(\lfloor144/4\rfloor=36\), and hence
\[
a(144)=2\cdot144+160+36=288+160+36=484.
\]

For \(m=157\) and \(k=175\), the relevant exact values are
\[
4\cdot175^2=122500,
\qquad
5\cdot157^2=123245,
\qquad
4\cdot176^2=123904.
\]
Therefore
\[
122500\le123245<123904,
\]
so
\[
175\le157\sqrt{\frac54}<176
\]
and
\[
\left\lfloor157\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=175.
\]
Moreover, \(157=4\cdot39+1\), whence \(\lfloor157/4\rfloor=39\). Thus
\[
a(157)=2\cdot157+175+39=314+175+39=528.
\]

Finally, for \(m=161\) and \(k=180\), we compute
\[
4\cdot180^2=129600,
\qquad
5\cdot161^2=129605,
\qquad
4\cdot181^2=131044.
\]
It follows that
\[
129600\le129605<131044,
\]
so
\[
180\le161\sqrt{\frac54}<181
\]
and hence
\[
\left\lfloor161\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=180.
\]
Since \(161=4\cdot40+1\), we have \(\lfloor161/4\rfloor=40\). Therefore
\[
a(161)=2\cdot161+180+40=322+180+40=542.
\]

We can now compare the two sides of the conjectured recurrence at \(n=140\). Its right-hand side is
\[
a(157)+a(144)-a(140)
=528+484-471
=1012-471
=541,
\]
whereas its left-hand side is
\[
a(161)=542.
\]
Thus
\[
a(161)=542\ne541=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
Since \(140\ge1\), this is an index at which the conjecture claims the equality must hold. The proposed recurrence therefore fails, and the universal conjecture is false.
